newsitem.title: USA: Clinton hails education as heart of balanced budget.
newsitem.headline: Clinton hails education as heart of balanced budget.

text.p: President Clinton, hailing the balanced budget agreement as an "historic accord," said Saturday he personally believed its major legacy lay in a renewed commitment to education.

"This agreement includes the most significant increase in education funding in 30 years," hsaid in his weekly radio address. "Even more important, it provides the largest single increase in higher education since the G.I. Bill in 1945, more than 50 years ago."

Clinton praised the accord -- reached Thursday after intense haggling between the White House and congressional leaders -- for expanding opportunity "so that we can keep the American Dream alive for all our children."

"To me, the heart of this balanced budget agreement is its historic commitment to education," he said. "Education has always been at the heart of opportunity in America. It's the embodiment of everything we have to do to prepare for the 21st century."

The legislation funds many of Clinton's pet projects, including the "America Reads" programme to mobilise volunteer tutors to ensure that every eight-year-old can read; the Technology Literacy Initiative intended to wire every classroom and school library into the Internet by 2000; and the HOPE Scholarship for tuition tax credit, designed to make the first two years of college as universal as high school.

Clinton said his goal for this budget was "to dramatically expand opportunity through education, to give all our children the tools to succeed in the new economy and the new society of the new century."
In the final agreement, which proposes to balance the federal budget by 2002, Clinton got a commitment for $35 billion for education tax credits and deductions.
In his radio address, the president also paid tribute to Republicans as well as Democrats for their efforts in hammering out the accord.
"Thanks to leaders in Congress in both parties who led the way, along with my negotiators, we have crafted an historic accord," he said.
Clinton credited economic policies of his first term for five years of deficit reduction. In 1993 the deficit was near $300 billion and this year it is estimated at $67 billion.

"We moved quickly back then to put in place a new policy -- a policy of invest and grow -- cutting the deficit, investing in our people, opening new markets around the world through tough trade agreeemnts," he said.
"The results of that strategy are now clear."

The budget plan cuts spending $304 billion more over the next five years than what would have occurred without changes in policy. Much of this comes from a $115 billion savings in Medicare and $14 billion from Medicare. It provides for a net $85 billion tax cut by 2002 and gives Clinton $33 billion for domestic goals.
The agreement goes to both houses of Congress for approval next week and Clinton urged lawmakers to pass it.
"Pass the balanced budget and pass the biggest and best education bill in America's history," he said.
